title: The Tragic Tale of Floyd Collins
summary: Josh and Chuck tell the story of Floyd Collins, a Kentucky cave explorer and guide who became trapped in Sand Cave near Mammoth Cave in January 1925. The episode covers the Kentucky Cave Wars among rival cave operators, Collins's early life and cave business, the collapse that pinned him, the rescue attempts by his brother Homer, reporter Skeets Miller, and the surrounding media circus, the failed shaft rescue after about two weeks, his death, the burial and later display of his body in Great Crystal Cave, the 1929 grave robbery, and his final reburial in 1989. It ends with a listener mail segment about the "nappuccino" coffee nap term.

segments.title: Tour announcement and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh announces spring 2023 tour dates and ticket link, then opens the show with banter about Kentucky tragic history and Barron County.

segments.title: Mammoth Cave and the Kentucky Cave Wars
segments.summary: The hosts describe Mammoth Cave's size and history, the enslaved guide Stephen Bishop's mapping, and the Kentucky Cave Wars, in which rival cave operators sabotaged each other with tactics like blocking roads and misleading tourists.

segments.title: Floyd Collins's early life and looting
segments.summary: Collins grew up near Mammoth Cave, left school at ten, and sold Native American artifacts from caves to tourists at the Mammoth Cave Hotel. He later found Great Crystal Cave but it was poorly located and not financially successful.

segments.title: Sand Cave and the chimney crawl
segments.summary: Collins leased Sand Cave on Cave City Road, a loose, muddy cave, and dug a passage through it. On January 30, 1925 he descended a ten-foot chimney and a tight crack into a chamber, then his lantern went out and a rock shifted and pinned his foot while he was climbing back.

segments.title: Early rescue attempts by Homer and Johnny Burnette
segments.summary: Collins was trapped in darkness and cold. His brother Homer and other locals tried to free him, with food and blankets sent down, while surgeons were offered money to amputate and the rescue was left to amateurs.

segments.title: Skeets Miller and the media circus
segments.summary: Louisville Courier Journal reporter Skeets Miller went into the cave to interview Collins and became a rescuer, bringing light and organizing a bucket brigade. His dispatches were picked up by the Associated Press and radio broadcasts, drawing thousands of spectators and carnival-style vendors.

segments.title: Collapse, failed shaft rescue, and Collins's death
segments.summary: Partial clearing gave Collins some movement, but the cave collapsed and cut off access. Officials brought in experts and steam shovels to dig a shaft over about 18 days, but Collins was found dead, likely several days earlier, and his body was left in place.

segments.title: Hoax rumors, Homer's fundraising, and burial
segments.summary: Rumors spread that the trapping was a stunt or a hoax, and a tribunal was convened. Homer toured on the vaudeville stage to raise money for a dig, and Collins was later buried in the family cemetery with a stalactite headstone.

segments.title: Body displayed in Great Crystal Cave, 1929 theft, and 1989 reburial
segments.summary: Harry Thomas, a dentist, bought Great Crystal Cave and put Collins's body in a glass coffin there. Grave robbers stole it in 1929 and the leg was lost, and the National Park Service closed public access after buying the site in 1961. A court ordered the body reburied topside in 1989.

segments.title: Cultural legacy: Ace in the Whole and the Floyd Collins musical
segments.summary: The hosts mention Billy Wilder's 1951 film Ace in the Whole, a media-focused take on the event, and a 1996 musical about Floyd Collins, which the hosts describe as a more respectful work.

segments.title: Listener mail: nappuccino
segments.summary: A listener's brother coined the term 'nappuccino' for a coffee nap, and the hosts react to it.
